<p>Welcome to UNC Charlotte and Niner Nation! The staff within the Division of Student Affairs are committed to your personal, educational, mental and physical success as students. Treating all students with care and respect is paramount.</p><p>There are plenty of opportunities for new and returning students. Join a <a href="https://greeklife.uncc.edu/">fraternity or sorority</a> or one of over 400 <a href="https://studentorgs.uncc.edu/">student organizations</a>. Cheer for the Niner Nation at an <a href="https://charlotte49ers.com/">Athletics</a> event. Zip around campus on an <a href="https://pats.uncc.edu/transportation/gotcha-e-scooters-and-bikes">E-scooter</a>. If you want to talk to someone about depression, anxiety, or relationship issues, contact <a href="https://caps.uncc.edu/">CAPS</a> (Christine F. Price Counseling and Psychological Services). If you do not have enough to eat, visit the <a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/">Jamil Niner Food Pantry</a>. For families who want to stay involved with campus happenings, the <a href="https://nsfs.uncc.edu/families/49er-family-hub">49er Family Hub</a> delivers the most current information to your inbox.</p><p>The more you put into your college experience, the more you will get out of it. And should you stumble or falter, we are here to help you recover. If you can’t find what you’re looking for on the website, contact me at baileyk@charlotte.edu or on Twitter at <a href="https://twitter.com/CLTVCSA">@CLTVCSA</a>.</p><p>Sincerely,</p><p>Dr. Kevin W. Bailey <br>Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs</p><hr><p> </p></div>

    	    <div class="section-title">
			<a id="CareersInStudentAffairs">Careers in Student Affairs</a>
		</div>
  
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p>Most students do not come to college knowing what student affairs is or that there is a rewarding career to be had in it. Whether you were an RA, peer mentor, fraternity or sorority member, intramurals sports competitor, building manager or tour guide you have already been exposed the field of student affairs. Annually, October is <a href="https://www.naspa.org/careers">Careers in Student Affairs</a> month where formal programs occur on college campuses to expose students to the field of student affairs. At UNC Charlotte, there is a <a href="https://catalog.charlotte.edu/preview_program.php?catoid=33&poid=8864">master's</a> and <a href="https://edld.uncc.edu/programs/edd-educational-leadership">doctoral</a> programs in Educational Leadership with an emphasis on Student Affairs. Many UNC Charlotte alumni have completed their undergraduate degrees then pursued a graduate degree in Student Affairs or Higher Education Administration as a result of the positive experience they’ve had at UNC Charlotte. Meet some of our alumni and read their student affairs stories below.</p></div>
            
			</section>
	</div>

      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">
                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">

                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p dir="ltr"><em><strong>Housing and Residence Life</strong></em></p><h3>Rewitzer Builds Community, Career Path at Charlotte</h3><p dir="ltr">By Wyatt Crosher, Assistant Director of Communications for Student Affairs</p><p dir="ltr">Growing up, Stephanie Rewitzer thought she knew exactly what career she was going to pursue.</p><p dir="ltr">“I was confident that I was going to go be a marine mammal trainer,” she said. “Probably with Shamu.” </p><p dir="ltr">That path remained when she went to the Florida Institute of Technology as an undergrad. But things changed, and Rewitzer found a new endeavor that would ultimately lead her to becoming associate director in UNC Charlotte’s Housing and Residence Life (HRL) years later.</p><p dir="ltr">“In my time at Florida Tech, I really got into housing, became an RA and ultimately became an undergraduate hall director,” Rewitzer said. “I found a passion for working in the halls and specifically being able to supervise students and eventually professionals in that area. That really launched me into a new trajectory.”</p><p dir="ltr">Rewitzer applied to graduate school at Florida State to study higher education administration. That led to her first professional role at Georgia Southern. She started as a resident director before transitioning to an assistant director position. </p><p dir="ltr">When it came time to move closer to family in North Carolina, Rewitzer said Charlotte stood out.</p><p dir="ltr">“I just really enjoyed the culture and the people,” she said. “The focus on students, particularly with emphasis on acknowledging the different populations we have within our students, was really exciting to me. I also appreciated having some of the resources of a larger institution, but at a University that still felt small enough to make connections.”</p><p dir="ltr">Rewitzer has been at Charlotte since June 2019. She arrived on campus as assistant director and now is the associate director for academic initiatives and staff training programs within HRL.</p><p dir="ltr">While Rewitzer said the day-to-day of her position is constantly shifting, the standout moments are when she gets to work with students and her peers in a way that brings them all together.</p><p dir="ltr">“Some of the favorite things I get to do at Charlotte connect me back to what brought me in, which is that sense of community,” Rewitzer said. “I really enjoy the opportunities to go join a field day that's happening out in the quad or a student-staff appreciation event. I get excited to get out there and engage in that way.”</p><p dir="ltr">One of Rewitzer’s responsibilities in HRL has involved working on the back end of Niner Chats, a once-per-semester check-in that allows residents an opportunity to talk with resident advisors (RAs) about whatever is on their minds.</p><p dir="ltr">Her work within Niner Chats, and assessment work for HRL overall, earned Rewitzer the Assessment Champion honor at last year’s Student Affairs End-of-Year Awards. It was an award Rewitzer was excited about, both for being noticed on more behind-the-scenes efforts, but also because the award represented a larger successful partnership between HRL and the Student Affairs Research and Assessment (SARA) team.</p><p dir="ltr">“It was really rewarding to see that it made an impact and that others recognized that effort,” Rewitzer said. “SARA really supports us every time we have questions. The award coming from partners and people that I get to consistently work with and see them do really wonderful work just made it all the more special.”</p><p dir="ltr">While it’s not the career path she planned her whole life, Rewitzer has found a path that works for her over nearly five years at Charlotte. Her advice to anyone facing a similar crossroads is to maintain an open mind and be open to change as it comes.</p><p dir="ltr">“I think looking around and finding what you're passionate about and being willing to pursue that while also thinking about the logistics of that,” she said. “I didn't know this was a career path until I was a senior, so be comfortable to chart your course and do what you need to do to align with what you ultimately want.”</p></div>

	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><h3>McGrew Makes Impact on Food Insecurity at Charlotte</h3><p>By Wyatt Crosher, Assistant Director of Communications for Student Affairs</p><p>Matthew McGrew is in just his second year at UNC Charlotte, but this sophomore in the <a href="https://engr.charlotte.edu">William States Lee College of Engineering</a> has already sparked positive changes in the lives of students on campus.</p><p>In his sophomore year, McGrew became student champion and ambassador for the <a href="https://ninerpantry.charlotte.edu">Jamil Niner Student Pantry</a> in the Collegiate Hunger Challenge. In part thanks to McGrew’s efforts, <a href="https://studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/unc-charlotte-wins-collegiate-hunger-challenge-2022">Charlotte won the challenge</a>, earning $10,000 to support initiatives like purchasing fresh produce, bread and eggs at the pantry on a weekly basis.</p><p>All of it started because of an assignment in the <a href="https://honorscollege.charlotte.edu">University Honors</a> Colloquium class, one of the first McGrew took at the University, where he was tasked with finding out about places on campus.</p><p>“Because of that, I went to the food pantry and volunteered there,” McGrew said. “I really enjoyed it, so I kept volunteering."</p><p>McGrew has enjoyed his time with the pantry, both for the people he’s able to work with and for those he’s able to serve. He said food insecurity — a lack of consistent access to enough food for a person to live an active, healthy life — is an important issue that he wants to help with any way possible.</p><p>"Food insecurity impacts a lot of people on campus, even if you don't realize it,” McGrew said. “It's good to know my work is helping students get through college a little bit easier."</p><figure role="group" class="caption caption-drupal-media align-right">

<div class="wide">
  
  
                  <div class="field field--name-field-image field--type-image field--label-hidden field__item">    <picture>
                  <source srcset="/sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_large_2x/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=NrZQhOV4 1x, /sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_large_2x/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=NrZQhOV4 2x" media="all and (min-width: 1200px)" type="image/webp" width="2400" height="1350">
              <source srcset="/sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_large/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=iI3IYItq 1x, /sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_large_2x/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=NrZQhOV4 2x" media="all and (min-width: 992px) and (max-width: 1199px)" type="image/webp" width="1280" height="720">
              <source srcset="/sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_medium/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=70Hblw-5 1x, /sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_large/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=iI3IYItq 2x" media="all and (min-width: 767px) and (max-width: 991px)" type="image/webp" width="720" height="405">
              <source srcset="/sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_small/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=3C8WP-W1 1x, /sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_medium/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=70Hblw-5 2x" type="image/webp" width="480" height="270">
                  <img loading="eager" width="1280" height="720" src="/sites/studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/files/styles/16_9_large/public/image/Matthew%20Pantry.jpg.webp?h=d318f057&itok=iI3IYItq" alt="Matthew McGrew smiling behind a load of groceries at the Jamil Niner Student Pantry">

  </picture>

</div>
            
</div>

<figcaption><em>McGrew at the Jamil Niner Student Pantry</em></figcaption>
</figure>
<p>Before getting involved with the pantry, McGrew came to Charlotte from Raleigh because of how much he enjoyed the campus and its proximity to the city. He is majoring in electrical engineering with the goal to work on power grids.</p><p>McGrew became interested in electrical engineering after the power grid crisis that occurred in Texas in 2021, which left more than 4.5 million homes and businesses without power for multiple days. He also felt a reaction to the shooting attack on North Carolina’s Moore County power grid, which left up to 40,000 residential and business customers without electrical power, as another reason why he chose this field of study.</p><p>"I knew I wanted to do some sort of engineering, and the power grid issues in Texas and North Carolina just ensured that I wanted to make the power grid more reliable," McGrew said. “I’m planning on concentrating on power energy systems while I’m here, and I want to go into working with the power grid when I go into the industry."</p><p>Outside of his major, McGrew also plays the baritone in Charlotte’s <a href="https://marchingband.charlotte.edu">Pride of Niner Nation Marching Band</a>. He said joining the band made sense after doing so in high school, and it has helped him find a great group of friends.</p><p>With his time at Charlotte nearing the halfway point, McGrew said his current goals are to continue doing the things he has enjoyed with the University thus far: pursuing his major, working with the pantry and performing in the marching band.</p><p>Regardless of where he ends up, McGrew said his intention is to continue making a difference involving food insecurity after he leaves the University.</p><p>"I plan to continue helping with food insecurity after I graduate,” McGrew said. “I'm not sure if I'll be in Charlotte or Raleigh at that point, but it's important to me to help."</p><p><em>For more information on the Jamil Niner Student Pantry, visit the </em><a href="https://ninerpantry.charlotte.edu/"><em>pantry’s website</em></a><em>.</em></p><p><br> </p></div>

      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">

	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><div class="field__item"><em><strong>Popp Martin Student Union</strong></em></div><h3>Barnhill Honored After More Than a Decade at UNC Charlotte</h3><p>By Wyatt Crosher, Communications Coordinator for Student Affairs</p><p>There’s something about a fresh coat of paint that makes a building feel brand new. It is also an important part of any maintenance plan to keep student-fee funded facilities looking and operating at their best, a task that takes many hands.</p><p>These jobs can sometimes go unnoticed. But Randy Barnhill, maintenance technician at the Popp Martin Student Union, had his efforts recognized at the Student Affairs End-of-Year Celebration in May with the Above and Beyond Award for facilities support.</p><p>According to the written nomination:</p><p>“We can often hear Randy Barnhill working before we see him. In the early hours of the morning before students occupy every chair in the Student Union, Randy is listening to music while painting. Painting the walls in the stairwells green, repainting the places we have all run into with our backpacks or carts, covering up the fingerprints on the walls, and making sure the railings are smooth so no one cuts their hands on jagged paint.</p><p>“Over the past year in particular, Randy has painted the enormous walls in the staircases as the Popp Martin Student Union team updates the Union and brings in more UNC Charlotte icons throughout the facility. He has been instrumental in the project, bringing green throughout the building to highlight particular spaces.”</p><p>His supervisor, Ernest Purifoy, maintenance supervisor, adds, “Randy is a hard worker and is very detail oriented.” </p><p>Barnhill’s efforts past his job description were noted, including his positive demeanor and selfless attitude.</p><p>“Randy’s work doesn’t stop with the maintenance and improvements he brings to the Popp Martin Student Union. He is also incredibly welcoming and supportive of the students and University community in general,” the nomination stated. “He will stop what he is doing to grab the door for someone and he makes sure to acknowledge you whenever he sees you. Randy helps make the Popp Martin Student Union feel like a community.”</p><p>Barnhill has been at the University as long as the Student Union has, arriving at Charlotte when the doors were opened in 2009. Prior to that, he had worked a variety of side jobs.</p><p>The move made sense for him at the time, and has continued to be a job he’s enjoyed for the past 13 years.</p><p>"It's been really cool for a house painter,” Barnhill said. “It's been good having a stable, steady job with good benefits. All of it has been perfect for a guy my age."</p><p>Barnhill said it was surprising to win the Above and Beyond Award because, to him, everything he does for the University is business as usual.</p><p>"It was nice to hear,” he said. “I try to stay busy, but I really don't feel like I go above and beyond. I just stay busy and try to earn my keep."</p><p>Family is a key passion for Barnhill outside of work. He said he’s “become quite a family man” thanks to his three kids and seven grandchildren.</p><p>Over 13 years at Charlotte, Barnhill has seen the Popp Martin Student Union continue to evolve, both in its decor and with the students that come through the doors each day. And, even though awards aren’t usually his thing, Barnhill said it was gratifying to win the award for his hard work.</p><p>"It was cool to get appreciation,” Barnhill said. “I'm not really a guy that's into recognition, it’s not something I need, but it’s cool. It was a surprising honor and very nice to hear.”<br> </p></div>

                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p>By Wyatt Crosher, Communications Coordinator for Student Affairs</p>

<p>While Patty Cox has only been at UNC Charlotte as an assistant director for Student Niner Media since January, her efforts before arriving at the University have earned national recognition.</p>

<p>Cox, who came to Charlotte after a decade working at the Weather Channel, earned awards for three stories she helped produce as editor in chief. The videos all focus on climate change and the impact it is having around the world. It is an issue that Cox said is more prominent now than people may think.</p>

<p>"There is no climate change debate. It's a contentious topic, but there should be no debate,” Cox said. “Ninety-seven percent of climate scientists agree that it's here, it's happening and that, unfortunately, we are the ones that cause it. Communities all over are feeling its impact; It's no longer a thing that's in the future.”</p>

<p> </p></div>

                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p> </p>

<p>The first of the award-winning videos is <a href="https://features.weather.com//disaster-road/">“Disaster Road,”</a> which focuses on a stretch of highway in the south that has dealt with multiple natural disasters, at least in part due to climate change. It won first place in the online video 10 to 30 minutes category for the <a href="https://www.headlinerawards.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/2022-headliner-winners.pdf">National Headliner Awards</a>.</p>

<p>“We had covered the series of storms as they were happening, as well as the Texas freeze,” Cox said. “While you can't say that this particular hurricane is caused by climate change, we know that climate change is leading to more extreme weather, and that's what we were seeing with these events and that's what we wanted to spell out in that series."</p>

	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p> </p>

<p>Finally, <a href="https://features.weather.com/climate-change/">“Climate Change 101”</a> is as the title states: an information guide for all the important ideas on climate change. This video won a <a href="https://www.spj.org/sdxa21.asp">Sigma Delta Chi Award</a>, given out by the Society of Professional Journalists, for best video from a specialized journalism site.</p>

<p>"We were aware that people were searching for credible, simple information on climate change, so we put that together,” Cox said. “It's not aimed at teachers necessarily, but we thought it would give teachers a good primer on the issue."</p>

<h3>An Impressive Path to Charlotte</h3>

<p>These honors signified a strong ending to nearly a decade of Cox’s efforts at the Weather Channel, where she started as a content manager before moving up to executive editor and, eventually, editor in chief.</p>

<p>Before the Weather Channel, Cox worked at the Tampa Bay Times for more than two decades, ultimately becoming managing editor while leading a major redesign of the newspaper, as well as the publication’s <a href="https://www.tampabay.com">website</a>.</p>

<p>Cox left her position at the Weather Channel in January, coming to the University with nearly 40 total years of experience in the news industry. She did so both because of a change in location and a change in heart.</p>

<p>"My husband's career led us to Charlotte, but I was running my team remotely because of the pandemic, and I was going to commute to Atlanta where the Weather Channel is based,” Cox said. “I started working remotely, got the team moved to work remotely, and I thought I could do it, but I really missed interacting with people. I also wanted to get to a point where I was contributing to the future in some way, and I saw this role as an opportunity to do that.”</p>

<p>In her first six months at Charlotte, Cox said she has really enjoyed seeing the student journalists in Student Niner Media develop their writing and editing abilities.</p>

<p>"It really is a great student-run organization. It's been a thrill seeing light bulbs go off when you coach them,” Cox said. “It's student run and student done, but there are three advisors who will offer advice, coach through issues and then critique afterward. It's a great organization with a lot of good resources."</p>

<p>Cox worked her way up through the world of journalism, earning awards for her efforts along the way. Now, she is at Charlotte, ready to help the next generation of journalists. Her advice for anyone interested in joining the field starts with a few simple tips.</p>

<p>"Read, read, read and have an insatiable curiosity,” Cox said. “That's the best advice I have."</p>

<p><em>Learn more about Student Niner Media <a href="https://media.charlotte.edu">here</a>.</em></p></div>

            <h3 class="green"><span class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Casey Tullos, Ed.D.</span>
</h3>

      
              
  <div class="field field--name-field-position field--type-string field--label-visually_hidden">

                    <div class="field__item">Associate Vice Chancellor</div>
                </div>

      
              
      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">
                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p>Dr. Tullos discovered her passion for Student Affairs work as an undergraduate student at the University of South Alabama where she earned a bachelor of science degree in Management with a concentration in Human Resources. Her advisors encouraged her to pursue a master's degree at the University of Georgia, where she was introduced to the variety of opportunities available as a university housing officer. Upon completion of her master's degree in 1997, Dr. Tullos began her professional career at UNC Charlotte as the Residence Education Coordinator for Holshouser Hall.</p><p>Since beginning her career in Housing and Residence Life, Dr. Tullos has had the opportunity to grow and develop alongside the University. In 2011, she completed her doctorate in Adult and Community College Education at NC State University while working full-time as an Assistant Director. She served as Director of Residence Life at Winthrop University for a short period of time before returning to UNC Charlotte in 2018 as the Director of Residence Education. Dr. Tullos was appointed Interim Associate Vice Chancellor in June 2019, accepting the permanent role of Associate Vice Chancellor in January 2021.</p><p><br> </p><p class="btn btn-green"><a href="/senior-leadership-team" title="Back to Senior Leadership">Back to Senior Leadership</a></p></div>
            
			</section>

                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p>Each August, UNC Charlotte kicks off the academic year by welcoming new and returning students to campus with a week of programming called Gold Rush (formerly Week of Welcome). Gold Rush begins Friday, Aug. 16, with the Union Takeover at 7 p.m. and will run through Sunday, Aug. 25, with the National Pan-Hellenic Council Yard Show.</p><p>More than 50 events are part of this year’s <a href="https://nsfs.uncc.edu/gold-rush/about-gold-rush">Gold Rush</a>, including 12 signature events; Gold Rush is designed to instill Niner Pride, teach campus traditions and expose students to campus resources and opportunities for involvement.</p><p>Signature events are:</p><ul><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/recfest_2019?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHQzy2ZNBx">RecFest 2019</a>, 2 to 4 p.m., Sunday, Aug. 18, Northeast Recreational Field Complex</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/494_new_year_kickoff?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHQ5y2ZNBw">49er New Year and Kickoff Concert featuring Ari Lennox</a>, 5 to 8 p.m., Sunday, Aug. 18, Barnhardt Student Activity Center and West Quad</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/new_student_convocation_ceremony?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHRLy2ZNBw">New Student Convocation</a>, 11 a.m. to noon, Monday, Aug. 19</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/student_organizations_showcase?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHRhi2ZNBw">Student Organizations Showcase</a>, 3:30 to 6 p.m., Monday, Aug. 19, CHHS/CoEd Plaza</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/university_career_center_hosts_the_plaza_party?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHRpS2ZNBw">University Career Center Plaza Party</a>, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., Tuesday, Aug. 20</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/wear_green_wednesday?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHR4y2ZNBw">Wear Green Wednesday</a></li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/university_transfer_center_t-shirt_swap?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHSAi2ZNBw">University Transfer Center T-Shirt Swap</a>, 9 to 11:30 a.m., Wednesday, Aug. 21, Belk Plaza</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/the_game_of_life_college_edition?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHSKC2ZNBw">The Game of Life: College Edition</a>, 11:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., Wednesday, Aug. 21, Atkins Library Lawn</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/norms_quest_scavenger_hunt?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHSVi2ZNBw">Norm’s Quest Scavenger Hunt</a>, 3 to 5 p.m., Friday, Aug. 23, “49er Miner” (Norm’s Statue)</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/gold_rush_day_of_service?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHSfC2ZNBw">Gold Rush Day of Service</a>, 8 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., Saturday, Aug. 24</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/back_to_school_carnival?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHSvS2ZNBw">Back to School Carnival</a>, 5 to 8:30 p.m., Saturday, Aug. 24, SoVi Patio</li><li><a href="https://campusevents.uncc.edu/event/nphc_yard_show?utm_campaign=widget&utm_medium=widget&utm_source=University+of+North+Carolina+at+Charlotte#.XVHS4y2ZNBw">NPHC Yard Show</a>, 2 to 5 p.m., Sunday, Aug. 25, Star Quad</li></ul><p>All Gold Rush events are free for students and are hosted by UNC Charlotte campus departments and student organizations. Students can pick up Niner Pride T-shirts and Niner Pride Guides during Move-In.</p><p><em>This article originally appeared in </em><a href="https://inside.uncc.edu/news-features/2019-08-13/gold-rush-ushers-new-academic-year"><em>Inside UNC Charlotte</em></a><em>.</em></p></div>

	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p>Effectively immediately, <a href="https://studentaffairs.uncc.edu/about-us/senior-leadership/casey-tullos">Dr. Casey Tullos</a> is appointed the permanent Associate Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs (<a href="https://housing.uncc.edu">Housing and Residence Life</a>).</p><p>Casey began her career at UNC Charlotte 22 years ago as a Residence Education Coordinator (REC) in Holshouser Hall and has been promoted to positions of increasing authority and responsibility including Coordinator of Guest Operations and Assistant Director for Academic Initiatives and Staff Programs. She worked as Director of Residence Life at Winthrop University for a short period of time before returning to UNC Charlotte in 2018 to be the Director of Residence Education.</p><p>"Casey has been an admirable and capable leader of the department as interim AVC since the departure of Dr. Aaron Hart in June 2019," said Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Dr. Kevin W. Bailey. "Casey’s interim leadership included decision making around the future of the Phase XVI construction project, reviewing and expanding our residential living learning communities and strengthening our relationship with off campus apartment complex managers (including the Niner Choice Program)."</p><p>However, Casey’s most significant and challenging accomplishment has been managing housing during a pandemic. </p><p>No housing professional has prepared for a crisis in the form of a pandemic, yet Casey quickly adapted to the reality and has been the leader for such actions as de-densifying residence halls (thus reducing their occupancy and revenue by over half), coordinating a protocol to manage surge testing after a waste water signal has been detected, guiding the process to manage and answer the questions from anxious students and parents and keeping the morale of employees high as rules and conditions change regularly. </p><p>"Housing has been at the center of the University’s COVID-19 mitigation efforts and Casey has managed it all with grace, poise and professionalism. She has a great team who has met every challenge thrown their way with the health and safety of residents as paramount," Bailey said.</p></div>

	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p>By Wyatt Crosher, Assistant Director of Communications for Student Affairs</p>

<p>UNC Charlotte’s Niner Finances is partnering with the <a href="https://www.bap.org/">Beta Alpha Psi</a> honorary organization and <a href="https://www.vitalatino.org/what-is-vita">Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) Latino</a> to offer a pair of on-campus events focused on offering free tax preparation services.</p>

<p>“Being able to offer this important service to our community has been a goal of Niner Finances for some time now. Under the leadership of our assistant director Nicole Benford we are now able to bring this national program here on campus,” Dr. Brad Yeckley, director of Niner Finances, said. “In the coming years it is our intention to become an official IRS VITA site. This will allow us to expand our offerings while also training and developing students to become volunteers. We are grateful and fortunate to have been able to partner with a couple of amazing organizations this year, and we look forward to continuing these relationships as we grow this effort.”</p>

<p>The first event, taking place from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Saturday, March 18 in the University Career Center, is open to the broader Charlotte community, with an emphasis on Latinx students and community members.</p>

<p>The link to sign up for the March 18 event can be found <a href="https://www.signupgenius.com/go/10c0f44afaa23a4f5c52-uncc#/">here</a>.</p>

<p>The second event is on Saturday, April 1, also from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the University Career Center. This event is only open to Charlotte students.</p>

<p>The April 1 event sign-up link can be found <a href="https://www.signupgenius.com/go/10c0f44afaa23a4f5c52-uncc1#/">here</a>.</p>

<p>Students and staff interested in this free service must have a social security number or ITIN (W7), a valid photo ID and have an earned income of $57,000 or less.</p>

<p>Niner Finances provides programming, resources, education and guidance for financial success to University students in an effort to improve financial literacy. For more information, head to the <a href="https://ninerfinances.charlotte.edu/">Niner Finances website</a>.</p></div>

                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><div class="article-content node__content"><div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field__item"><p>One student’s idea recently sparked a chain of kindness on campus. Wanting to show appreciation for campus heroes in Police and Public Safety (PPS) and Emergency Management, a student in the Collegiate Recovery Community had the idea to make and deliver care packages to the two departments.</p><p>After hearing the idea, Cassidy Conway, the graduate assistant for the <a href="https://wellness.uncc.edu/recovery">Collegiate Recovery Community</a> jumped into action, helping to organize donations and assistance. More than 40 volunteers gathered in the Cone University Center last week to fill bags with handwritten notes and donations such as tissues, candy, hand sanitizer, granola bars, air fresheners and bottled water. The group then delivered the 74 care packages to the FM/PPS Building.</p><p>The Collegiate Recovery Community is a program administered by the UNC Charlotte Center for Wellness Promotion. The mission of the Collegiate Recovery Community is to provide a nurturing, affirming environment in which students recovering from addictive disorders can successfully pursue academic, personal and professional goals for the purpose of enhancing their quality of life and becoming productive members of society.</p><p><em>This article originally appeared in </em><a href="https://inside.uncc.edu/news-features/2019-07-02/expression-appreciation-%E2%80%98hands-our-heroes%E2%80%99"><em>Inside UNC Charlotte</em></a><em>.</em></p></div></div></div>

      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">
                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p dir="ltr"><em><strong>Housing and Residence Life</strong></em></p><p dir="ltr"> </p><h3>Jordan Slomianyj Travels the World, Returns Home to Charlotte</h3><p dir="ltr">By Wyatt Crosher, Assistant Director of Communications for Student Affairs</p><p dir="ltr">For most staff members at UNC Charlotte, if they’re not at work, they can be found at home, perhaps even somewhere around the city. For Jordan Slomianyj, Residence Education Coordinator in Housing and Residence Life (HRL), if he’s not at his office in Witherspoon Hall, guessing his location could be as difficult as pointing randomly to the right spot on a map.</p><p dir="ltr">Slomianyj (pronounced “slow-me-on-knee”) has traveled to around 70 countries spanning all across the globe. He took that to new extremes on a recent expedition to Antarctica, a trip that earned Slomianyj the honor of visiting every continent before the age of 35.</p><p> </p><p dir="ltr"><strong>Early Explorations</strong></p><p dir="ltr">How did Slomianyj start his journey to dozens of countries and every continent on Earth? It began at an early age. </p><p dir="ltr">Born in Chapel Hill, Slomianyj grew up only a few hours from the University, but when he was about 8 years old, he moved to South Africa with his mother and stepfather. He lived there for two years before they ultimately moved back to the United States.</p><p dir="ltr">Fast forward to Slomianyj’s mid-twenties when he found himself at a career crossroads. Slomianyj decided then to work odd jobs and plan a trip around the world. This would take him backpacking through 10 countries in total, including a successful trek through Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay. But, after a quick stop at home, things hit a snag two months later.</p><p dir="ltr">While in Bali — a province of Indonesia — Slomianyj came down with dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness that is prominent in more tropical areas. Along with a high fever and muscle pains, it can also be life threatening.</p><p dir="ltr">“I got so sick that I was bedridden for 10 days, and this is while I'm by myself in a foreign country,” Slomianyj said. “You just have to wait it out, that's how you treat dengue fever, there's not really medication for it.” He cut the journey short and began to consider new paths. </p><p dir="ltr"> </p><p dir="ltr"><strong>Journey to Higher Education</strong></p><p dir="ltr">Slomianyj started applying to graduate schools. He chose Western Carolina, his undergrad alma mater, and earned a master’s of education through the university’s Higher Education Student Affairs (HESA) program.</p><p dir="ltr">His desire to work in student affairs came from strong personal experiences he had with housing staff during his time as a college student.</p><p dir="ltr">“There were all these people that were in residence life that made a difference in my life somehow or someway,” Slomianyj said. “I thought the opportunity to go into res life was a really good one, especially if I wasn't specifically sure what I wanted to do, because I knew I wanted to serve students.”</p><p dir="ltr">Slomianyj worked at the Arkansas School for Mathematics, Sciences, and the Arts after earning his master’s, a position he enjoyed, but one that took him far from home. That’s how he ended up in Charlotte’s HRL department, where Slomianyj has worked since October 2021.</p><p> </p><p dir="ltr"><strong>Unfamiliar Territory</strong></p><p dir="ltr">Slomianyj’s most recent trip would take him to the southernmost location on the planet: a 15-day cruise that included about a week in Antarctica. The other days were spent going to and from the continent, along with a stop in the Falkland Islands.</p><p dir="ltr">How does Slomianyj recount his time on one of Earth’s least populated locations? Above all else, he said it’s difficult to find words for.</p><p dir="ltr">“I really struggle to describe it,” Slomianyj said. “You're going through these places, and you don't know if they've ever even been walked on. It's like you're going into a place that's uncharted, or at least it feels that way. It’s ridiculously windy all the time. It's so unforgiving and harsh. But at the same time, because it's untouched, it's both beautiful and indescribable.”</p><p> </p></div>
            
			</section>
	</div>

                              <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p dir="ltr"><em>Photo Credits: Courtesy of Jordan Slomianyj</em></p><p dir="ltr"> </p><p dir="ltr">Among the highlights from Slomianyj’s journey include a variety of penguins, one night sleeping in a tent on the continent instead of on the ship — a night Slomianyj said he “did not sleep a wink” because of the harsh winds and low temperature — and a moment walking on the ice that put into perspective how real and potentially dangerous the trip was.</p><p dir="ltr">"I go out on the ice, and the main guide, he yells 'Abort, everyone off the ice right now,' because it's starting to crack,” Slomianyj said. “Everyone gets off the ice, and I go up to my cabin, and I see the ice cracking while the guide is in a boat pushing the ice close so all these other staff members can get to safety. As soon as we pulled away, that piece of ice sank. It showed the human element of what they're doing and how scary and risky it is.”</p><p dir="ltr">Slomianyj made it through the trip unharmed and returned home in December. </p><p dir="ltr"> </p><p dir="ltr"><strong>On the Horizon</strong></p><p dir="ltr">With about 70 countries and seven continents down, there are still new countries he aspires to see. At the top of the list is Japan and South Korea, but another goal is to visit the five “-stans”: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. He also has a trip planned for South Africa in March. It will be the first time he’s back since living there 24 years ago.</p><p dir="ltr">For those interested in traveling to a foreign country, Slomianyj recommends enrolling in the <a href="https://step.state.gov/">Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, or STEP</a>. He also uses the <a href="https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/traveladvisories/traveladvisories.html/">U.S.’ travel advisory scale</a> to help with the risk assessment on future journeys.</p><p dir="ltr">As a traveler who has gone to Brazil, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Slovenia and Thailand, just to name some of his favorite’s, Slomianyj has been able to see the world from a variety of angles. He said all of these experiences help him connect with the students he works with in his position.</p><p dir="ltr">"I think it helps relatability. I don't even need to have been to the place that you are from, but if I know something about it or I've heard of it, and make someone feel just a little bit more comfortable here,” Slomianyj said. “A lot of what we do in our job is mediation and conflict resolution, so it gives me skills to deal with that, and also to be aware of cultural differences and have better cultural awareness.”</p><p dir="ltr">Along with that, after making it through scenarios like surviving a 10-day bout with dengue fever or the harsh overnight conditions of Antarctica, Slomianyj also feels prepared for any situation that arises.</p><p dir="ltr">“If I think of the craziest situations that I've ever had while traveling,” Slomianyj said, “I don't think that anything I've encountered so far with work can even come close.”</p></div>

                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p dir="ltr"><em><strong>Student Involvement</strong></em></p><p dir="ltr"> </p><h3>Adam Burden brightens up campus with an award-winning program</h3><p>By Teagan Welch, Assistant Director of Communications for Student Affairs</p><p> </p><p dir="ltr">Adam Burden wasn’t expecting to receive the 2022-2023 Student Affairs Outstanding Program/Initiative Award for the "Light Up the Lake" program. But, when he found out he had won, he attributed the victory to the support from the people around him.</p><p dir="ltr">“To pull off these things, you can’t do it all by yourself. It really is a team effort to make everything come to life,” he said.</p><p dir="ltr">As the Director of Student Involvement at Charlotte, Burden wears many hats. Back in 2022, he pioneered the Light Up The Lake program. It is an event that happens in the fall semester, just before winter break. Students come together to mingle, drink hot cocoa, and see the Hechenbleikner Lake on campus illuminated by thousands of tiny green, white and gold lights. </p><p dir="ltr">Although it is a fun event for students and staff alike, the people working behind the scenes, like Burden, work hard to put it all together.</p><p dir="ltr">“I was literally stringing [holiday] lights up myself; definitely put some blood sweat and tears into it.”</p><p dir="ltr">For Burden, receiving the award for Light Up the Lake meant a lot, but there was more to celebrate. </p><p dir="ltr">“I was happy that other people saw the value and purpose behind what we were trying to do,” Burden stated. “The award is nice, but seeing the event catching on and sort of becoming a tradition on campus is very rewarding too.” </p><p dir="ltr">Burden has worked in Student Involvement at Charlotte for 10 years now. He says the best part of being a part of the Niner community is seeing the impact he has on the students. </p><p dir="ltr">“I have always thought of our office as the place that helps students make positive memories of their college experience,” he said. “When we host a large event, and there’s a ton of students out there connecting, there’s a feeling of togetherness and community and that makes me really happy to see.”</p><p dir="ltr">Burden says he loves working at Charlotte because he’s able to come up with new ideas and actually be celebrated for that.</p><p dir="ltr">“It’s a school where you feel like you can make an impact or make a change,” he explained. “I appreciate the willingness to be creative and do something with it.”</p><p dir="ltr"> </p>

      <svg class="svg-inline--fa fa-calendar-days fa-fw" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" data-prefix="far" data-icon="calendar-days" role="img" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 448 512" data-fa-i2svg=""><path fill="currentColor" d="M152 24c0-13.3-10.7-24-24-24s-24 10.7-24 24V64H64C28.7 64 0 92.7 0 128v16 48V448c0 35.3 28.7 64 64 64H384c35.3 0 64-28.7 64-64V192 144 128c0-35.3-28.7-64-64-64H344V24c0-13.3-10.7-24-24-24s-24 10.7-24 24V64H152V24zM48 192h80v56H48V192zm0 104h80v64H48V296zm128 0h96v64H176V296zm144 0h80v64H320V296zm80-48H320V192h80v56zm0 160v40c0 8.8-7.2 16-16 16H320V408h80zm-128 0v56H176V408h96zm-144 0v56H64c-8.8 0-16-7.2-16-16V408h80zM272 248H176V192h96v56z"></path></svg><!-- <i class="far fa-calendar-alt fa-fw"></i> Font Awesome fontawesome.com -->

  <div class="article-content">
          
      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">
                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><div class="article-content node__content"><div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field__item"><div class="align-center">The referenced media source is missing and needs to be re-embedded.</div><p>By: Jennifer Howe</p><p>The Jamil Niner Student Pantry is fully stocked for the first time, thanks to the generosity displayed by Niner Nation during this year’s #GivingTuesday campaign. More than $56,000 in monetary gifts and food donations was raised, ensuring that 49er students have the resources they need this holiday season and beyond. </p><p>"We’re thankful for everyone who participated in #GivingTuesday events to raise food and funds for the Jamil Niner Student Pantry," said Mindy Sides-Walsh, director of leadership & community engagement. "Many campus food pantries have either closed or been forced to limit their support over the past nine months. Due to the generosity of so many, we'll be able to fulfill the food needs of our students over the next year."</p><p>One in three college students experience food insecurity. The Jamil Niner Pantry has remained open during the COVID-19 pandemic and is serving more students than ever before. Client numbers have doubled since March and the pantry is receiving more food requests from nontraditional students with families, who are using the pantry for the first time.</p><h2>VIRTUAL FOOD DRIVE</h2><p>In addition to monetary gifts, this year’s campaign featured a virtual food drive. Alumni, faculty, staff and friends were encouraged to shop for items on the pantry’s <a href="https://www.amazon.com/registries/custom/6WYMPR8CJUB0/guest-view">Amazon wish list</a>, including peanut butter, oatmeal, lentils, canned fruit and beans. More than 14,000 items were purchased from the list, with a total value of $19,629.</p><p>"Thank you to all the alumni, faculty and staff for not only spreading the word for the virtual food drive but for also donating," said Nick Sulak ‘17. "Your donations are going to make an enormous difference and because of you, the pantry is stocked up and ready for students for the coming months."</p><h2>AXED RECIPE CHALLENGE</h2><p>Members of Niner Nation also created unique recipes, using at least two of the most-needed items from the Jamil Niner Student Pantry, which included canned chicken, canned fruit, healthy cereal, salad dressing, jelly and pasta sauce. The Axed Recipe Challenge participants were Andrew Baker ’15, Kristin Coffey ’20 and Rachael Forester, Rodney Graves ’97, Tahlieah Sampson ’22 and CJ ’13 & Samantha ’11 White.</p><p>Alumni, students, faculty, staff and friends of UNC Charlotte were encouraged to vote for a fan favorite 49er dish by making a donation to the <a href="http://giving.uncc.edu/">#GivingTuesday</a> campaign. Rodney Graves ’97 received the most votes for his Niner Nuggets and Miss Bonnie’s Blackberry FroYo. </p><p>"#GivingTuesday was another great example of the phenomenal things that Niner Nation can accomplish when we work as one," said Rodney Graves ’96.</p><p>Chadwick Boyd ’93, food and lifestyle expert and judge on Hallmark channel helped choose an overall best recipe for the challenge. "There was lots of creativity, great combinations of flavor and lots of enthusiasm," said Boyd, in reference to the recipe submissions. The overall best recipe was awarded to Tahlieah Sampson ’22, this year’s student body president for her Niner Noodles dish.</p><p>"I have always been raised to give back," said Tahlieah Sampson. "Life is not easy, especially right now. As Student Body President, I wanted to use my platform to amplify the pantry and explain how important it is to give back."</p><h2>MORE WAYS TO SUPPORT THE JAMIL NINER STUDENT PANTRY</h2><ul><li>Gifts can be made to the pantry throughout the year by visiting <a href="https://crowdfund.uncc.edu/project/20432">crowdfund.uncc.edu</a>.</li><li>Donate needed non-perishable food items. Visit the <a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/get-involved/donate">pantry’s website</a> for a list of needed food items and hours of operation.</li></ul><h2>ABOUT #GIVINGTUESDAY</h2><p>#GivingTueday, celebrated the Tuesday after Thanksgiving, is a global movement unleashing the power of people and organizations to transform their communities and the world. Created in 2012 as a day that encouraged people to do good, #GivingTuesday inspires hundreds of millions of people to give, collaborate and celebrate generosity.</p><p><em>This article originally appeared on </em><a href="https://inside.uncc.edu/news-features/2020-12-03/niner-nation-answers-call"><em>Inside UNC Charlotte</em></a><em>.</em></p></div></div></div>

            <div class="headline mb-2">
        
  <div class="field field--name-field-subhead field--type-string field--label-visually_hidden">
    <div class="field__label visually-hidden">Headline</div>
                    <div class="field__item">Business Services Specialist</div>
                </div>

      </div>
      
      <div class="content node__content">
                  
      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">
                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p><em><strong>Housing and Residence Life</strong></em></p><p> </p><p class="heading3" dir="ltr">Wendy Moore’s Commitment to Care</p><p dir="ltr"><br>By Megan Khor, Student Communications Assistant for Student Affairs</p><p dir="ltr">For Wendy Moore, the most meaningful part of her work isn’t found in titles or recognition, but in the everyday interactions that make her workplace feel supported and connected. </p><p dir="ltr">As the business services specialist in Housing and Residence Life, Moore is known for her patience, kindness and willingness to help. It is these qualities that helped Moore secure the 2024-2025 Positive Impact Award for Student Affairs. </p><p dir="ltr">“I enjoy working with people. It’s fulfilling to be able to do that and to know that somebody else appreciates what you do.” Moore said.</p><p dir="ltr">Moore’s path to Charlotte began when her husband, Doug Moore, encouraged her to apply for a job opening three years ago. Doug works as a facilities and maintenance supervisor, and he also received recognition with an Above and Beyond award in 2019.</p><p dir="ltr">Wendy recalls Doug saying, “Why don’t you apply for the job upstairs?” After two interviews, Moore earned the position. Nervous to do the best that she could in her new role, Moore recalled talking to a lot of people to see what they needed from her, as well as what she needed from them.</p><p dir="ltr">“It was fun building that rapport, and I am still very fond of the ones that have already come and gone onto new positions,” Moore said. “[For] family and friends, relationships are very important. I think what you get out of a relationship is what you put into it, no matter what that relationship is.”</p><p dir="ltr">Today, Moore processes all the bills, invoices and transactions made by the Residence Education Coordinators (RECs) at UNC Charlotte. </p><p dir="ltr">Within her role, she works most with the P-card office on campus and Concur, a web-based system that manages business travel, entertainment expenses and P-card reconciliation. Introduced in 2024, Concur created a steep learning curve for everyone who used the system. </p><p dir="ltr">Motivated to understand this new system and to help her colleagues through this shift, Moore took notes during the training classes offered by Concur whenever she could. Afterwards, she’d always made an effort to share what she learned with her colleagues. </p><p dir="ltr">“I didn’t realize when I read that [the nomination], that they thought I was instrumental in helping with that. I felt like I was just doing my job. Like I was doing what I should be doing to help them do their job,” Moore said.</p><p dir="ltr">Determined to spread what she had learned, Moore also co-facilitated a professional development session for the Residence Life professional staff to teach them how to use Concur. Following the session, she held one-on-one sessions with staff who needed extra guidance, walking them step by step through filing reports.</p><p dir="ltr">“It’s like telling somebody how to drive a car or putting somebody behind a steering wheel. You’re going to remember if you’re the one driving,” Moore said. </p><p dir="ltr">Beyond the trainings, Moore’s approachable and patient nature shows in the day-to-day. Colleagues often stop by her office not just for help with work tasks, but because they know they’ll be met with understanding and care.</p><p dir="ltr">“I know for me, I find myself gravitating to her office just to talk with her … She has a way of making people feel good without saying anything in particular,” Moore’s award nomination said. “Even when explanations need repeating, she does so with patience and a genuine desire to help others understand and feel confident.”</p><p dir="ltr">Last spring, during the end-of-year divisional meeting where the awards were announced, Moore recalled listening to the Positive Impact Award’s criteria. She remembered wondering who the recognition would go to until her own name was called. </p><p dir="ltr">“I think I just paused a minute,” Moore said. “I got a little emotional because I felt like somebody else noticed the things that I’m doing.”</p><p dir="ltr">She was especially surprised because she felt like her efforts weren’t something that was extraordinary. </p><p dir="ltr">“I was just doing my work … I want to be the best business services specialist I can be for them,” Moore said. “It touched my heart honestly … I’m very grateful for that award.”</p><p dir="ltr">Spending so much of her day at work, Moore believes its important to get along with the people you share that time with, and she’s grateful to be a part of a team where those relationships come naturally.</p><p dir="ltr">That same heart for those around her extends beyond campus and into Moore’s life at home. A proud grandmother, Moore keeps photos of her grandkids in her office that act as a reminder of the family and relationships that ground her. </p><p dir="ltr">Whether at work or at home with her grandkids, Moore approaches every relationship with the same care, patience and attention. It’s this consistent commitment to people through small gestures, thoughtful guidance and everyday support that truly defines her impact at Charlotte.</p><p dir="ltr">“I’m thankful to be here and to work here,” Moore said. “It’s a good environment.”</p></div>

                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p><strong>University Commendation for Leadership and Service Recipient</strong></p><p dir="ltr">Kamryn Latino is graduating with a degree in business administration. A dedicated member of the Zeta Gamma chapter of Alpha Delta Pi, she served as director of philanthropy and president, and represented her chapter nationally on the Collegiate Advisory Committee. She launched the Greater Charlotte Gala, raising $44,000 for Ronald McDonald House, and led Hurricane Helene relief efforts for Operation Airdrop, earning her the National Collegiate Philanthropy Volunteer Award and back‑to‑back campus service honors. Latino is also co‑founder of Greenway Girls, a women’s wellness, safety and fitness organization.</p></div>

  <div class="article-content">
          
      <div class="field field--name-field-content field--type-entity-reference-revisions field--label-hidden field__items">
                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><div class="article-content node__content"><div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field__item"><h4>By: Susan Messina</h4><p>Food insecurity affects students on U.S. college campuses at a rate that is often higher than twice that of the general population. UNC Charlotte is no exception; in fact, during the 2017 fall semester, 303 students visited the<a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/"> Jamil Niner Student Pantry</a>, located near main campus at 1224 John Kirk Drive.</p><p>“People are often surprised to hear that a significant number of students have trouble affording food, sometimes compromising their food needs to pay rent,” said Sean Langley, assistant director of leadership and community engagement. “UNC Charlotte addresses the issue head on, year-round and through activities and volunteering by students, faculty and staff during<a href="https://hhweek.org/"> National Homelessness and Hunger Awareness Week</a>.”</p><p><a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/">The Jamil Niner Student Pantry</a>, in operation since 2014, operates year-round, provides food donated by UNC Charlotte students and parents,<a href="https://www.foodlion.com/in-our-community/food-lion-feeds/"> Food Lion</a>,<a href="http://www.chartwellshighered.com/"> Chartwells</a>, and the community. It’s named for benefactor and UNC Charlotte trustee <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rUQINgcKd_o">Dhiaa Jamil ’78</a>, executive vice president and chief operating officer, Duke Energy, who experienced food insecurity as a UNC Charlotte student.<a href="https://ninerengage.uncc.edu/account/create?returnUrl=/event/2874139"> Students, faculty and staff may volunteer </a>at the pantry year-round, Monday through Thursday, 1:45 to 3:15 p.m., or 3:30 to 5 p.m., serving as greeters, shelf stockers, housekeepers, gardeners or thank-you-note writers.</p><p><a href="http://www.swipehunger.org/uncc">Swipe Out Hunger</a> allows UNC Charlotte students with a meal plan to<a href="https://volunteer.uncc.edu/swipe-out-hunger"> donate meal swipes from their 49er ID card</a> to students who are facing food insecurity. Students who need to utilize the program can complete an assessment with<a href="https://sass.uncc.edu/services/meal-swipes-program"> Student Assistance and Support Services</a>. (In addition, students can apply declining balance at Outtakes or SoVi Market + Bakery to purchase Hunger Relief Packs for $25 or $49 to donate to their fellow students.) Another national program,<a href="https://campuskitchens.org/"> Campus Kitchens</a>, operates at UNC Charlotte with food service provider Chartwells. Since 1991, Chartwells has donated food after events to local homeless shelters and food pantries. This fall, that effort expanded to provide food to the Jamil Niner Student Pantry.</p><p><strong>Check out these special opportunities during National Homelessness and Hunger Week:</strong></p><ul><li><strong>Monday, Nov. 12, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.—Hunger and Homelessness Week Kickoff</strong>. Stop by<a href="https://aux.uncc.edu/news/south-village-crossing-%E2%80%93-it%E2%80%99s-so-different"> SoVi</a> or<a href="https://aux.uncc.edu/dining/dining-halls"> Crown Commons Dining Hall</a> to donate <a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/get-involved/donate">needed items</a> to the Jamil Niner Student Pantry. Learn about<a href="https://leadership.uncc.edu/swipe-out-hunger"> Swipe Out Hunger</a> and<a href="https://www.foodlion.com/in-our-community/food-lion-feeds/"> Food Lion Feeds</a>, and sign a pledge to participate throughout the week. Sponsored by the<a href="https://leadership.uncc.edu/community-engagement"> Office of Leadership and Community Engagement</a></li><li><strong>Tuesday, Nov. 13, and Thursday, Nov. 15, 6 to 8 p.m.—Volunteer at</strong><a href="https://www.secondharvestmetrolina.org/"> <strong>Second Harvest Metrolina</strong></a>. Student, faculty and staff volunteers will sort and stock food at this community-based organization committed to fighting hunger locally. To sign up, email Autumn Robertson, arobe126@uncc.edu. Transportation is available</li><li><strong>Wednesday, Nov. 14, CHHS, Room 147, 6 to 8 p.m.—Niner Discussion: Understanding Hunger and Homelessness in Charlotte. </strong>Sean Langley, who co-founded the Jamil Niner Student Pantry with Kim Buch, Department of Psychological Science, will lead a discussion prior to the showing of <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2013/02/14/172040074/documentary-a-place-at-the-table-is-a-call-to-action-on-hunger">“A Place at the Table,”</a> a documentary that highlights the stories of three Americans struggling with food poverty and outlines a way to solve hunger in the United States. No reservations needed</li><li><strong>Thursday, Nov. 15, 11 p.m. to 2 a.m., CHHS/COED Courtyard—“Sleep Out.”</strong> Simulate (in a safe setting) the experience of those who live and sleep outdoors. Cardboard boxes will be provided; bring coats, hats, gloves appropriate for the weather</li><li><strong>Friday, Nov. 16, 1 to 2 p.m.,—Tour Niner Student Pantry (1224 John Kirk Drive).</strong>Students, faculty and staff are invited to learn more about the ways UNC Charlotte is combating food insecurity on campus</li><li><strong>Support </strong><a href="https://www.foodlion.com/in-our-community/food-lion-feeds/"><strong>Food Lion Feeds</strong></a><strong>—</strong>When faculty, staff and students download the<a href="https://www.foodlion.com/mvp-program/food-lion-mobile-app/"> Food Lion app</a> or obtain a Food Lion MVP card (or send their MVP Card number to <a href="mailto:volservices@uncc.edu">volservices@uncc.edu</a>), and  shop at Food Lion, 9323 N. Tryon Street, UNC Charlotte earns one point for every $10 spent for a chance to win $10,000</li></ul><p><strong>Learn More:</strong></p><ul><li>See ar<a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/about-us/related-articles">ticles and videos about the issue of hunger among college students and UNC Charlotte’s  effort</a></li><li><a href="https://ninerpantry.uncc.edu/about-us/related-articles">Read “</a><a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B7JiwrcCdBGUSU8taVoyM3ZYcUVGT21ud1VDZW9ZWTFobVY0/view">A University-Community Partnership to Combat Food Insecurity among College Students</a>,” coauthored by Kim Buch, Sean Langley, Tamara Johnson and Nakiel Coleman</li><li><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QT-fj4Ioeps">Alumna Robin Emmons</a>, is founder of <a href="https://www.sowmuchgood.org/">Sow Much Good</a>, a nonprofit organization that grows environmentally friendly crops to combat hunger in the Charlotte area</li><li>Beth Racine, Department of Public Health Sciences, is<a href="https://www.wsoctv.com/news/9-investigates-thousands-in-charlotte-struggle-to-find-healthy-food-options/863025125"> featured on WSOC-TV</a> in regard to “food deserts” in Charlotte</li></ul><p><em>This article originally appeared in </em><a href="https://inside.uncc.edu/news-features/2018-11-07/fight-hunger-unc-charlotte-during-homelessness-and-hunger-awareness-week"><em>Inside UNC Charlotte</em></a><em>.</em></p></div></div></div>

                      <div class="field__item">	<div class="paragraph paragraph--type--text paragraph--view-mode--default">
    
    	
	<section>
					
                  <div class="clearfix text-formatted field field--name-field-body field--type-text-long field--label-hidden field__item"><p dir="ltr">On Monday, Nov. 6, UNC Charlotte was named as one of 325 schools in the Military Times 2023 <a href="https://studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/unc-charlotte-named-military-times-best-vets-college-rankings">Best for Vets college rankings</a>. This is the third consecutive year Charlotte has been ranked.</p><p dir="ltr">The Military Times survey is sent to colleges and universities across the nation asking about their programs for veterans. The survey results are analyzed, along with public data about colleges and universities obtained from the Department of Education and Department of Veterans Affairs, and turned into an official ranking. </p><p dir="ltr">Schools were asked to complete the survey earlier this year and the responses were then analyzed by the Military Times data team. The ranking is the largest and most comprehensive annual ranking of schools for military service members and veterans.</p><p dir="ltr">Best for Vets highlighted Charlotte’s “high-value, high-quality education to a diverse population of more than 30,000 students.” It also emphasized the University’s various services for veterans, including its career services tailored to military students, and its various mental health services, including on-campus counselors trained in military-related mental health issues.</p><p dir="ltr">Charlotte has also <a href="https://studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/unc-charlotte-retains-gold-status-military-friendly-schools-list">earned the Military Friendly School Gold Award</a> for two consecutive years It was one of 250 universities nationally to earn the honor in March out of more than 1,800 participating schools. In addition, Charlotte rose 22 spots in U.S. News & World Report's Best Colleges for Vets 2024 ranking.</p><p dir="ltr">The University is currently <a href="https://studentaffairs.charlotte.edu/unc-charlotte-celebrates-veterans-week-nov-6-10">celebrating Veterans Week</a>, with multiple on-campus events leading up to Veterans Day on Saturday, Nov. 11. </p><p dir="ltr">More information on how UNC Charlotte supports the success of its military-affiliated student body can be found <a href="https://veterans.charlotte.edu/">on the VSO website</a>.</p></div>
